result.reason: The passage is the mishnah text itself (nadra vehi arusa, nisgaresh bo bayom, etc.), which is precisely what the 'Mishnah: Vows' section's prose describes and analyzes in detail.

Both items constitute the Gemara's question and initial answer about whether the last groom can annul vows already disclosed to the first groom — precisely the content described in candidate 1's prose about 'niru le'arus rishon' — while the current placement (candidate 2) describes Shmuel's verse proof and the challenge, which comes after the question is already posed.

The passage is the baraita text itself ('tanya kavasei deShmuel'), which the 'Braita Opening' section (index 1) explicitly introduces as the complex baraita the Gemara cites in support of Shmuel — the prose there describes the opening of this exact baraita including 'na'arah hame'urasah aviha veba'alah meferin nedareha', matching the passage's content perfectly as an introduction to the whole baraita before it is broken into sub-scenarios.

Both items directly present the Beit Shammai vs. Beit Hillel dispute — item 1 introduces the disagreement and item 2 explains the reasoning of each school — which is precisely what the 'Beit Shammai vs Hillel' prose section discusses, and the passage currently sits there correctly.
The passage raises the exact dilemma 'gerushin k'shtika damya o k'hakama damya' which is precisely what section 3 ('Gerushin Status Q') introduces and discusses.

All five items form a single continuous Talmudic chain debating whether gerushin is like shtika or hakama — beginning with the nafka mina of divorce-and-remarriage (item 1), then the baraita proofs and counter-proofs (items 2-4), and concluding with the mishnah proof about repeated betrothals (item 5) — all of which is precisely what the 'Divorce & Remarriage Case' prose describes as the Gemara's attempt to resolve this question from a braita and then a mishna.

Both items are the Gemara's challenge-and-answer sequence about why the mishnah specifies 'that day' if the first arus never heard the vow, and the resolution that the father's hearing drives the same-day requirement — exactly the content described in the 'Mishnah Qualification' prose.

The passage presents the mishna text and its immediate conclusion ('learn from this that divorce is like ratification'), which matches heading 0's prose describing exactly this ta shema proof, before the elaboration in heading 1 and the counter in heading 2.

The passage presents the Gemara's rejection that the mishna deals with a nesuah and that the reason for inability to annul is 'ein haba'al meifer bekodmin', which is precisely what the 'Nesuah Objection' prose describes.
